concept_note.title: Overfitting: Regularisation, Dropout, and Early Stopping
concept_note.summary: Overfitting is not inevitable. Regularisation techniques — dropout, weight decay, data augmentation, early stopping — push models toward generalisation.
learning_goals: Understand regularisation as a penalty on complexity
Read L2 weight decay and dropout in code
Understand data augmentation and early stopping
concept_note.long_intro: You know that overfitting is a real problem. Now let us talk about how to fight it. There are four main defences, and every serious training pipeline uses at least two of them. Regularisation adds a penalty for large weights, discouraging the model from depending too much on any single feature. Dropout randomly disables neurons during training, forcing the model to be robust. Data augmentation creates variations of your training examples, effectively increasing dataset size. Early stopping watches the validation loss and halts training when it starts to rise. Together these techniques are what make modern deep learning work at all.

deep_explanation.heading: L2 regularisation (weight decay)
deep_explanation.body: L2 regularisation adds a penalty proportional to the sum of squared weights to the loss. This discourages the model from having large weights, which in turn discourages it from relying on any single input feature too heavily. The penalty strength is controlled by a hyperparameter λ (lambda). In PyTorch, L2 regularisation is built into the optimizer as weight_decay. Values around 1e-4 to 1e-2 are typical. Too little and the model overfits; too much and it underfits.
deep_explanation.code:
# Loss with L2 regularisation
# loss_total = loss_data + lambda * sum(w^2)

weights = [0.5, -0.3, 0.8]
lam = 0.01

loss_data = 0.42
l2_penalty = lam * sum(w ** 2 for w in weights)
total_loss = loss_data + l2_penalty

print(f"data loss: {loss_data}")
print(f"L2 penalty: {l2_penalty:.4f}")
print(f"total loss: {total_loss:.4f}")

deep_explanation.heading: Dropout
deep_explanation.body: Dropout randomly sets a fraction of neuron activations to zero during each training step. This prevents neurons from co-adapting — a neuron cannot rely on the specific presence of another neuron because that other neuron might be dropped out next step. At test time, dropout is turned off. This simple trick has become a standard regulariser in almost every deep network. Typical dropout rates are 0.1 to 0.5, with higher rates for larger models.
deep_explanation.code:
import random

def dropout(activations, rate=0.5):
    if not activations:
        return activations
    scale = 1.0 / (1.0 - rate)
    return [
        a * scale if random.random() > rate else 0.0
        for a in activations
    ]

random.seed(42)
acts = [0.8, -0.5, 0.3, 1.2]
print("original:", acts)
print("after dropout:", dropout(acts, rate=0.5))

deep_explanation.heading: Data augmentation
deep_explanation.body: Data augmentation creates variations of your training examples. For images, this might mean flipping, cropping, rotating, or changing brightness. For text, it might mean synonym replacement or back-translation. The augmented examples are not new information, but they force the model to be invariant to those transformations. A model that has seen the same cat both upright and rotated is less likely to overfit to the specific orientation of the training set. Augmentation is one of the highest-return investments in practical ML.

deep_explanation.heading: Early stopping
deep_explanation.body: Early stopping is the simplest regulariser: watch the validation loss, and stop training when it stops improving. Save the model at the epoch with the best validation performance. This requires no change to the model or loss function — just patience and a stopping criterion. Typical patience is 3-10 epochs without improvement. Early stopping is not a replacement for other techniques; it is used alongside them. But it is often the easiest way to gain 2-5% accuracy on a task.
deep_explanation.code:
def train_with_early_stopping(epochs, patience=3):
    best_loss = float("inf")
    best_epoch = 0
    no_improvement = 0

    # Placeholder test losses
    test_losses = [0.9, 0.6, 0.4, 0.35, 0.37, 0.42, 0.50, 0.60]

    for epoch in range(epochs):
        val_loss = test_losses[epoch] if epoch < len(test_losses) else 1.0
        if val_loss < best_loss:
            best_loss = val_loss
            best_epoch = epoch
            no_improvement = 0
        else:
            no_improvement += 1
            if no_improvement >= patience:
                print(f"Stopped at epoch {epoch}")
                break

    return best_epoch, best_loss

print(train_with_early_stopping(8, 3))

concept_note.formal_definition: Overfitting mitigation techniques fall into four categories: (1) parameter regularisation (L1, L2, weight decay) penalises large weights; (2) structural regularisation (dropout, batch norm) introduces noise or normalisation during training; (3) data-level augmentation expands the effective training set; (4) training-process control (early stopping, learning rate schedules) stops or slows training when generalisation starts to degrade. Most production models combine at least two of these.

code_example.universal_explanation: This is the shape of every serious PyTorch training loop. Dropout sits inside the model. Weight decay is passed to the optimizer. Early stopping wraps the epoch loop. Together they produce models that generalise instead of memorise.

common_mistakes: Using dropout at inference time: dropout is only applied during training. At test time, all neurons are active.
Setting weight decay too high: it prevents the model from learning the signal at all, leading to underfitting.
Relying on only one regulariser: dropout, weight decay, and augmentation work best together.
Stopping training based on training loss: early stopping must monitor validation loss, not training loss.
concept_note.real_world_usage: Every modern deep learning pipeline uses these techniques. GPT models use weight decay and dropout. Image classifiers use aggressive data augmentation (random crops, flips, colour jitter). Speech recognition uses time-shift and pitch-shift augmentation. Even fine-tuning a pretrained model usually involves a small learning rate plus early stopping based on validation loss. When you read a research paper, the 'implementation details' section almost always lists which regularisers were used and at what strength.
key_takeaways: L2 regularisation penalises large weights; built into most optimizers as weight_decay.
Dropout randomly disables neurons during training, making the model robust.
Data augmentation expands the effective training set with transformations.
Early stopping watches validation loss and halts when it starts to rise.
Modern training pipelines combine multiple regularisers.

activity.question: What happens to dropout at inference (test) time?
choices: It is applied at the same rate as during training
It is turned off — all neurons are active
It is applied twice as strongly
activity.reveal: Dropout is only active during training. At test time, all neurons contribute, and their outputs are scaled to compensate for the training-time scaling.

activity.question: Validation loss decreases until epoch 5, then rises for 3 epochs straight. With patience=3, what does early stopping do?
choices: Stops at epoch 8, keeping the model from epoch 5
activity.reveal: Patience of 3 means stop after 3 consecutive epochs without improvement. Best model was at epoch 5; training runs 6, 7, 8 (three non-improving epochs), then stops.

activity.code:
# PyTorch model
model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(784, 256),
    nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Dropout(0.3),
    nn.Linear(256, 10),
)

# Test time
model.eval()
model.train()   # ← this line should not be here
output = model(test_input)
activity.explanation: Line 10 calls model.train() right before inference. This switches dropout back on, corrupting the test prediction. During evaluation, the model must stay in eval mode (which the previous line set). Remove model.train().

test.question: A model overfits on a small dataset. Which combination is likely to help most?
choices: Adding dropout, weight decay, and data augmentation
Training for more epochs with the same setup
test.reveal: Combining multiple regularisers is the standard remedy. Adding capacity or training longer makes overfitting worse.
